units.text: Establishment of image-guided radiotherapy of orthotopic hepatocellular carcinoma mouse model

mice in situ to mimic the pathological characteristics of the original HCC.Tumor formation was monitored by applying magnetic resonance imaging techniques and verified by H&E histopathological staining, AFP staining, and Ki67 staining.A single dose of 10 Gy X-ray was applied to simulate clinical radiotherapy plans using image-guided radiotherapy (IGRT) equipment.The efficiency of radiotherapy was then assessed by examining tumor size and weight one week after radiation.Cleaved-caspase3 staining and TUNEL were used to assess apoptosis in tumor tissues.

Results: Intrahepatic tumor development was detected in the liver according using MRI.A high-density shadow could be seen 10 days after cell injection, which indicated the formation of HCC in vivo.The tumors grew steadily bigger, and underwent precision radiotherapy 20 days after injection.The typical pathological characteristics of HCC, such as large, deeply stained nuclei and irregular cell size, were visible with H&E staining.After radiotherapy, significantly higher expression of the immunohistochemical markers Ki67 and AFP were detected in tumor tissue than in the nearby normal tissue.Compared with the control group, the tumor volume (p = 0.05) and weight (p < 0.05) of the irradiated group were significantly reduced.In addition, a higher frequency of apoptosis was identified in irradiated HCC tumor tissue using the TUNEL and cleaved-caspase3 staining assay.
Conclusions:
In a well-established orthotopic HCC model, MRI was utilized to monitor the formation of tumors, and IGRT was used to simulate clinical radiotherapy.
The present study could provide a suitable preclinical system for HCC radiotherapyrelated studies.

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the seventh most common cancer in the world, 1 and accounts for 75%-85% of primary liver cancer cases. 2,3The pathogenesis of HCC is thought to be related to chronic infection with the hepatitis B and C viruses (HBV and HCV), obesity and alcoholism, among other causes. 2The common treatment options for HCC include transcatheter arterial chemoembolization (TACE), radiofrequency ablation, and surgical resection. 46][7] For example, the application of stereotactic body RT (SBRT) and proton beam therapy (PBT) ensure that high doses of radiation can be delivered to the target while sparing surrounding normal tissue. 8vertheless, there is no industry-wide agreement on the fractionation method, fractionation dose, combination of radiotherapy with other therapeutics, or schedule of treatment for HCC.Neither is there a standard protocol for HCC radiotherapy.Therefore, a stable preclinical model is needed to facilitate related clinical studies.

Currently, HCC animal models can be categorized as chemically induced models, genetically engineered models (GEMs), xenograft models, and syngeneic models. 9First, chemically induced models can be used to reveal mechanisms of carcinogenesis but the time to tumor induction is too long.GEMs make it possible to study specific proteins and signaling pathways on HCC, but the low tumor mutation burden and high cost have been obstacles to applying GEMs. 10 Xenograft models often partially or completely exclude the influence of the immune system on radiation therapy and lead to some biases.Finally, syngeneic models not only have the advantage of a short time to tumor induction but also take the influence of the immune system after radiotherapy into consideration.

In previous mouse models, radiotherapy was mostly performed by shielding the surrounding tissues, and the irradiation position was mostly based on anatomical position estimation.In the present study, the X-RAD SmART small animal image-guided radiotherapy system, which uses the CT scanning unit to monitor tumors and healthy organs in real time, was adopted before and during the treatment of small animals.This system enables the modification of the treatment conditions in response to changes in the position of the organs, so that the irradiation field closely resembles the target area, increasing the treatment's accuracy. 10The benefit is that the geographical location, shape, and size of the tumor within the body may be precisely evaluated using three-dimensional CT imaging.Using this information, a precise radiotherapy plan can be created, allowing X-rays to be targeted to the tumor's location and irradiation from various angles. 11llectively, this study provides a reliable modeling technique
| Cell culture

The murine HCC cell line Hepa1-6 was purchased from BNCC(BNCC, China), cultured in DMEM (Hyclone) supplemented with 10% FBS (BI), 100 U/mL penicillin G, and 100 mg/mL streptomycin (Beyotime) in an incubator under 5% carbon dioxide atmosphere at 37°C in a relative humidity of 95%.
| Orthotopic HCC mice model construction

All animal studies were performed according to protocols approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Soochow University.C57BL/6 mice (6-8 weeks) were anesthetized with isoflurane.After disinfection of the skin with iodophor solution, a 1 cm incision was made along the medioventral line below the breastbone to expose the liver.Then, 1 × 10 6 Hepa1-6 cells mixed 1:1 with Matrigel matrix (Corning) in 30 μL of mixture were slowly injected into the liver, followed by abdominal closure.tumor reached a maximum of 1 cm, orthotopic HCC mice were treated with 10 Gy X-rad (X-RAD SmART; OMIXYS).Seven days later, the mice were sacrificed, and the tissues were removed.
| Dynamic imaging monitoring of orthotopic HCC
| Image-guided radiotherapy of HCC mice

Execution of the radiotherapy plan using a single dose of 10 Gy X-ray was accomplished by applying an X-RAD SmART system (OMIXYS, USA) following the manufacturer's protocol.In brief, mice were anesthetized with 1.5% isoflurane, followed by cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) image acquisition and reconstruction.Inbuilt SmART Plan software enabled construction of an accurate plan, visualization, and ultimately optimization of the treatment dose prior to therapy.Dose distribution and dose volume histograms (DVH) were computed to validate that 95% of tumor tissue can be irradiated with 9.5 Gy or more, and the remaining 5% can be irradiated with 10.4 Gy using a 10-mm collimated arc beam at 225 kV, 20 mA; the total irradiated dose was 10 Gy.

| Immunohistochemistry

The tissue sections were paraffin-embedded after being treated with 10% neutral-buffered formalin.Following an epitope retrieval approach, 3 μm paraffin slices were deparaffinized and heated in citrate buffer (pH 6.0) for 7 minutes.Cleaved-caspase3 (SAB, China, 29034) and AFP (SAB, China, 25163) primary antibodies were incubated at 4°C overnight on 3 μm paraffin sections before being incubated with biotinylated secondary antibodies (Beyotime).Using a diaminobenzidine and hydrogen peroxide-containing substrate solution, immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining was accomplished.
Hematoxylin was used for counterstaining.The entire process was carried out at room temperature. 13
| Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT)-mediated dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) assay

Upon genomic DNA breakage, the exposed 3′-OH can be catalyzed by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) plus biotin-dUTP, followed by horseradish peroxidase streptavidin-HRP, and finally, DAB color development catalyzed by HRP to reveal apoptotic cells.Paraffin sections from the control and irradiated groups were subjected to TUNEL assay by using the Beyoncé Apoptosis Detection Kit according to the user manual.Briefly, after treatment of paraffin sections with Proteinase K, the sections were incubated for 60 min at 37°C with the prepared TdT plus biotin-dUTP protected from light, followed by incubation with streptavidin-HRP and DAB at room temperature for 30 min, separately.Finally, the chromogenic cells were observed by light microscopy and analyzed.
| Statistical analysis

Data are presented as means ± SEM and SPSS 22.0 software (SPSS Inc.) was used.Numerical data were analyzed using Student's t test and the difference was considered significant when the p value was <0.05.
| RE SULTS
| Establishment of orthotopic HCC models

A batch of mice was established using the protocol described above (Figures 1A and 2A).To confirm tumor formation, the presence of highdensity T2-weighted imaging signaling in the liver of tumor-forming mice was observed by MRI.The tumor was visible on the MRI image 10 days after the injection, but was small in size; the tumor then grew significantly every 5 days compared to the previous 5 day period.As shown in Figure 2B, on the twentieth post-injection day, tumors were visible and large in size, generally greater than 200 mm 3 .Furthermore, pathological slices of the tumor showed that the cells were aberrant.The characteristics of the original implanted cancer cells were retained, with a large nucleus, deep staining, various cell sizes, and irregular morphology (Figure 3A).
| Assessment of effects of radiotherapy

The mice (n = 6) with orthotopic tumors were randomly split into two groups.The mice were treated according to the above image-guided radiotherapy protocols; the total radiation dose was 10 Gy at a dose rate of 2 Gy/min (Figure 4A).There was a clear trend towards tumor volume reduction after irradiation (p = 0.05) (Figures 4B and 5A)
Tumor weight also decreased significantly after radiotherapy (p < 0.05) (Figure 5B).

Additionally, cleaved-caspase3 expression was higher in the irradiated tumor tissues compared to the unirradiated ones.Caspase-3 is a key player in apoptosis, and cleaved-caspase3 participates in the activation of other cysteine aspartic enzymes and apoptotic proteins, suggesting that apoptosis is much more likely to occur in irradiated tumor tissues than in the control group (Figure 5C).TUNEL analysis was used to examine apoptosis within tumor tissues more directly, and similar to the cleaved-caspase3 staining results, there were more cells with DNA breaks within the irradiated group's tissues, indicating that apoptosis occurred more frequently within the irradiated group.(Figure 5D) A comparison of tumor volume and weight between the two groups, together with the analysis of apoptosis in the tumor tissue, led to the conclusion that the tumor tissue was successfully treated with radiation.Currently, there are two primary techniques for the establishment of syngeneic models, hydrodynamic tail vein injection and orthotopic injection. 14,16The advantage of orthotopic injection over hydrodynamic tail vein injection is the big, single tumor development.Accordingly, we created orthotopic hepatocellular carcinoma models for our investigation.The model further allows for an in-depth understanding of the effects of radiotherapy on the tumor microenvironment.
| DISCUSS ION

To establish a non-invasive in vivo technique to monitor tumor development in mouse livers, we used magnetic resonance imaging to track the growth of tumors in mice.Magnetic resonance imaging is an efficient method for in vivo detection of intrahepatic tumor formation in animal models because of its high spatial resolution, clear anatomical imaging, and powerful functional imaging analysis. 17Considering that HCC is often accompanied by metastasis and one mouse in our model also developed intestinal metastasis, the model can also be used to study the abscopal effects of radiotherapy, as well as distal metastasis before and after radiotherapy based on MRI.

9][20] Multiple animal trials were required to validate the preliminary basic research on precision radiotherapy mixed with other cancer treatment approaches.To imitate the clinical aspect of radiation for patients with liver cancer, we chose a single dose of 10 Gy X-ray using the X-RAD SmART radiotherapy system for this study. 21 a study of HCC, researchers found that a single 10 Gy X-ray activated the immune function of mice more than a fractionated dose, resulting in a better outcome. 22Similarly, our data also provide a basis for subsequent studies of large fractionated irradiation for HCC treatment.

Although the present study successfully established imageguided radiotherapy of an orthotopic HCC mice model, there are also limitations.First, because of the weak localization capacity of CT for intrahepatic tumors, the tumor site is not apparent during radiotherapy, which makes it more challenging to define the target area.In this work, the target region was defined by adjusting the mice's body position, comparing the MRI data, and then appropriately extending the irradiation field.Second, no p-values below 0.05 were found in the tumor volume statistics between the irradiated and control groups.It is speculated that this result is due to two factors.The first is the small number of mice in each group, which results in a large effect of individual differences within the group.The second is that the volume of observed tumors was estimated by assuming the shape to be a hemisphere.However, while this estimation is reasonable for small tumors, tumors with large diameters tend to be flat in shape, resulting in larger estimated tumor volumes than the real data warrant.To resolve the latter issues in follow-up investigations, tumor measurements should be based on tumor weight, and the number of mice in each group should be increased to limit the interference of individual differences.We also believe that it may be possible to enhance the CT signal at the tumor site by using some CT contrast agents and to decrease inaccuracy in defining the target area by increasing the number of parallel samples within the group.

In conclusion, this model provides a relatively rapid and easyto-implement approach that allows for the refinement of preclinical research models for radiation therapy in HCC, and subsequent combination with mouse gene knockout technology allows for the investigation of the specific role of relevant genes in tumor radiotherapy, which may be critical for reducing radioresistance in HCC.
